Abstract.

We investigate the global time existence of smooth solutions for the Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto system of cross-diffusion equations of two competing species in population dynamics. If there are self-diffusion in one species and no cross-diffusion in the other, we show that the system has a unique smooth solution for all time in bounded domains of any dimension. We obtain this result by deriving global W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates of Calderón-Zygmund type for a class of nonlinear reaction-diffusion equations with self-diffusion. These estimates are achieved by employing Caffarelli-Peral perturbation technique together with a new two-parameter scaling argument.

1. Introduction and Main Results

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded open set in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with n≥2n\geq 2. We consider the following popular system of reaction-diffusion equations:

(1.1) {ut=Δ⁡[(d1+a11​u+a12​v)​u]+u⁡(a1−b1​u−c1​v)inΩ×(0,∞),vt=Δ⁡[(d2+a21​u+a22​v)​v]+v⁡(a2−b2​u−c2​v)inΩ×(0,∞),∂u∂ν→=∂v∂ν→=0on∂Ω×(0,∞),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)≥0,v⁡(x,0)=v0​(x)≥0inΩ,\left\{\ \begin{array}[]{lcll}u_{t}&=&\Delta[(d_{1}+a_{11}u+a_{12}v)u]+u(a_{1}-b_{1}u-c_{1}v)&\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ v_{t}&=&\Delta[(d_{2}+a_{21}u+a_{22}v)v]+v(a_{2}-b_{2}u-c_{2}v)&\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\vec{\nu}}&=&\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial\vec{\nu}}=0&\mbox{on}\quad\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)&=&u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0&\mbox{in}\quad\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where the coefficients ak,bk,ck,dka_{k},b_{k},c_{k},d_{k} are positive constants, while ai​ka_{ik} are non-negative constants, for i,k=1,2i,k=1,2. Hereafter, ν→​(⋅)\vec{\nu}(\cdot) denotes the unit outward normal vector field on the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega.

The system (1.1) was proposed by Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto in [30] to model the spatial segregation of two competing species in the region Ω\Omega. It is usually referred to as the SKT system of cross-diffusion equations. In (1.1), uu and vv are the population densities of the two species. The terms d1​Δ​u,d2​Δ​vd_{1}\Delta u,d_{2}\Delta v are the diffusion ones due to the random movements of individual species with positive diffusion rates d1,d2d_{1},d_{2}. Meanwhile, Δ⁡[(a11​u+a12​v)​u]\Delta[(a_{11}u~+~a_{12}v)u] and Δ⁡[(a21​u+a22​v)​v]\Delta[(a_{21}u~+~a_{22}v)v] come from the directed movements of the individuals toward favorable environments. The considered species hereby move away from the high population density to avoid the population pressure, hence ai​ka_{ik} are non-negative. The constants a11a_{11}, a22a_{22} are called self-diffusion coefficients, while a12a_{12} and a21a_{21} are cross-diffusion coefficients. The homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions mean that there are no movements across the boundary. We note that the zero order nonlinearities in (1.1) are reaction terms of the standard Lotka-Volterra competition type or Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovskii-Piskunov reaction type. Also the system (1.1) reduces to the well-known Lotka-Volterra system of predator-prey equations when ai​k=0a_{ik}=0 for all i,k=1,2i,k=1,2.

The system (1.1) has attracted interests of many mathematicians. We particularly refer the interested readers to the survey paper [38] and the books [24, 25, 37]. The local existence of non-negative solutions is established by H. Amann in the seminal papers [1, 2]. This result is summarized in the following theorem.

Theorem 1.1 ([1, 2, 3]).

Suppose n≥2n\geq 2 and ∂Ω\partial\Omega is smooth. Let p0∈(n,∞)p_{0}\in(n,\infty) and u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} be non-negative functions in W1,p0​(Ω)W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega). Then there exists a maximal time tmax∈(0,∞]t_{\textup{max}}\in(0,\infty] such that the system (1.1) has a unique non-negative solution in Ω×(0,tmax)\Omega\times(0,t_{\textup{max}}) with

u,v∈C⁡([0,tmax),W1,p0​(Ω))∩C∞​(Ω¯×(0,tmax)).u,~v\ \in\ C([0,t_{\textup{max}}),W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega))~\cap~C^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,t_{\textup{max}})).

Moreover, if tmax<∞t_{\textup{max}}<\infty then

(1.2) limt→tmax−[‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p0​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p0​(Ω)]=∞.\lim_{t\rightarrow t_{\textup{max}}^{-}}\Big[\left\|u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)}+\left\|v(\cdot,t)\right\|_{W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)}\Big]=\infty.

Many efforts have been made to investigate the existence globally in time of solutions for (1.1). In some special cases with very strong restrictions on the spatial dimension nn and the coefficients dk,ai​kd_{k},a_{ik}, i,k=1,2i,k=1,2, the solutions are proved to exist globally in time (see [10, 11, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 31, 32, 33, 36]). Despite these achievements, whether this full system possesses global time solutions or finite time blow up solutions remains challenging and vastly open, even for n=2n=2.

In this paper, we study the system (1.1) when there are self-diffusion in one species and no cross-diffusion in the other. Specifically, we investigate (1.1) when a11>0a_{11}>0 and a21=0a_{21}=0:

(1.3) {ut=Δ⁡[(d1+a11​u+a12​v)​u]+u⁡(a1−b1​u−c1​v)inΩ×(0,∞),vt=Δ⁡[(d2+a22​v)​v]+v⁡(a2−b2​u−c2​v)inΩ×(0,∞),∂u∂ν→=∂v∂ν→=0on∂Ω×(0,∞),u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)≥0,v⁡(x,0)=v0​(x)≥0inΩ.\left\{\ \begin{array}[]{lcll}u_{t}&=&\Delta[(d_{1}+a_{11}u+a_{12}v)u]+u(a_{1}-b_{1}u-c_{1}v)&\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ v_{t}&=&\Delta[(d_{2}+a_{22}v)v]\quad\quad\quad+v(a_{2}-b_{2}u-c_{2}v)&\mbox{in}\quad\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\vec{\nu}}&=&\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial\vec{\nu}}=0&\mbox{on}\quad\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ u(x,0)&=&u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0&\mbox{in}\quad\Omega.\end{array}\right.

The system (1.3) was studied in [10, 11, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 33, 34] where the global time existence is established either with some restrictive conditions on the coefficients or for small nn. For the latter, the result is proved by Lou-Ni-Wu [22] for n=2n=2, by Le-Nguyen-Nguyen [21] and Choi-Lui-Yamada [11] for n≤5n\leq 5, and by Phan [34] for n≤9n\leq 9. However, whether the solution of the system (1.3) exists globally in time for every dimension nn is still a well-known open problem. This question is on the list of open problems made by Y. Yamada in [38]. One main purpose of the current paper is to give it an affirmative answer. Precisely, we prove the following result:

Theorem 1.2.

Suppose n≥2n\geq 2 and ∂Ω\partial\Omega is smooth. Let a11>0a_{11}>0 and u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} be non-negative functions in W1,p0​(Ω)W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega) for some p0>np_{0}>n. Then the system (1.3) possesses a unique, non-negative global solution (u,v)(u,v) with

u,v∈C⁡([0,∞),W1,p0​(Ω))∩C∞​(Ω¯×(0,∞)).u,v\in C([0,\infty),W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega))\cap C^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,\infty)).

Let us discuss the main difficulties and our strategy of proving Theorem 1.2. Thanks to Theorem 1.1, it is sufficient to show that condition (1.2) for finite time blowup does not happen. It is known that this task could be achieved if one can obtain L∞L^{\infty}-estimates for the solutions uu and vv in finite time intervals. As there exists the maximum principle for the second equation in (1.3), the central issue is to establish the boundedness for uu. For this, the maximum principle is naturally of our first consideration. Unfortunately, such maximum principle is not available for the system and this presents a serious obstacle.

One possible approach to get around the lack of the maximum principle for the system is to exploit the first equation in (1.3) to get LpL^{p}-estimates for uu for sufficiently large pp. Since the Laplacian term in this equation can be expressed as ∇⋅[(d1+2a11u+a12v)∇u]+a12∇⋅[u∇v]\nabla\cdot[(d_{1}+2a_{11}u+a_{12}v)\nabla u]+a_{12}\nabla\cdot[u\nabla v], the approach is only plausible if one is able to show that ∇v∈Lp\nabla v\in L^{p} for large pp. However, this type of gradient estimates for vv is essentially not known. We would like to stress that the classical Sobolev regularity theory [14, 16, 23] as well as its very recent developments [4, 5, 6, 9, 26] cannot be applied to get W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates for vv due to the nonlinear structure in the second equation in (1.3). In previous studies, many authors tried to avoid dealing with this key issue by using De Giorgi-Nash-Moser techniques to establish CαC^{\alpha}-regularity for vv first. However for nonlinear equations of reaction-diffusion type in (1.3), this also requires the establishment of a priori LpL^{p}-estimate for uu for some p>(n+2)/2p>(n+2)/2. In general, obtaining such LpL^{p}-estimate for uu is not known and challenging unless one assume that n≤9n\leq 9. This is the main reason that limits the known works such as [11, 17, 22, 21, 33, 34, 36] to small dimension nn only.

Our purpose is to tackle directly the problem of obtaining LpL^{p}-estimates for ∇v\nabla v in terms of LpL^{p} norms of uu. We establish new global W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates of Calderón-Zygmund type that are suitable for the scalar nonlinear diffusion equation appearing in (1.1). This is our second goal of the paper which is also a topic of independent interest in view of recent developments in [4, 5, 6, 9, 14, 19, 16, 23, 26]. Not only does it help to prove Theorem 1.2, we believe that our result on W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates also gives some insight into the structure of equations in (1.3) that is not known before. For the scaling and transformation invariant reason that will be explained below, we study equations in more general form than the one in (1.3).

For any fixed T>0T>0, we consider the following class of nonlinear parabolic equations:

(1.4) {ut=∇⋅[(1+αλu)𝐀∇u]+θ2u(1−λu)−λθcuinΩT:=Ω×(0,T],∂u∂ν→=0on∂Ω×(0,T),u⁡(⋅,0)=u0​(⋅)inΩ,\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcll}u_{t}&=&\nabla\cdot[(1+\alpha\lambda u)\mathbf{A}\nabla u]+\theta^{2}u(1-\lambda u)-\lambda\theta cu&\text{in}\quad\Omega_{T}:=\Omega\times(0,T],\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\vec{\nu}}&=&0&\text{on}\quad\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\ u(\cdot,0)&=&u_{0}(\cdot)&\text{in}\quad\Omega,\end{array}\right.

where α≥0\alpha\geq 0, θ,λ>0\theta,\lambda>0 are constants, and c⁡(x,t)c(x,t) is a non-negative measurable function. We also assume that

(1.5) {𝐀=(ai​j):ΩT→ℳn×nis symmetric, measurable, and there existsΛ>0 such that:Λ−1​|ξ|2≤ξT​𝐀​(x,t)​ξ≤Λ​|ξ|2for almost every (x,t)∈ΩT and all ​ξ∈ℝn.\left\{\begin{split}&\mathbf{A}=(a_{ij}):\Omega_{T}\to{\mathcal{M}}^{n\times n}\ \text{is symmetric, measurable, and there exists}\ \Lambda>0\mbox{ such that:}\\ &\Lambda^{-1}|\xi|^{2}\leq\xi^{T}\mathbf{A}(x,t)\xi\leq\Lambda|\xi|^{2}\quad\mbox{for almost every\ $(x,t)\in\Omega_{T}$ and all }\xi\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}.\end{split}\right.

Here ℳn×n\mathcal{M}^{n\times n} is the linear space of n×nn\times n matrices of real numbers. Our goal is to derive global W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates for weak solution uu of (1.4) for a general class of 𝐀\mathbf{A} and a general domain Ω\Omega. To state the result, we need the following definitions.

Definition 1.3.

Given R>0R>0. Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} be a function from ΩT\Omega_{T} to ℳn×n\mathcal{M}^{n\times n}. We define

[𝐀]B​M​O​(R,ΩT)=sup0<ρ≤Rsup(y,s)∈ΩT¯1|Kρ​(y,s)|​∫Kρ​(y,s)∩ΩT|𝐀⁡(x,t)−𝐀¯Bρ​(y)∩Ω​(t)|2​𝑑x​𝑑t,[\mathbf{A}]_{BMO(R,\Omega_{T})}=\sup_{0<\rho\leq R}\sup_{(y,s)\in\overline{\Omega_{T}}}\frac{1}{|K_{\rho}(y,s)|}\int_{K_{\rho}(y,s)\cap\Omega_{T}}{|\mathbf{A}(x,t)-\bar{\mathbf{A}}_{B_{\rho}(y)\cap\Omega}(t)|^{2}\,dxdt},

where Kρ(y,s)=Bρ(y)×(s−ρ2,s]K_{\rho}(y,s)=B_{\rho}(y)\times(s-\rho^{2},s] is a parabolic cube and 𝐀¯U​(t)=⨏U𝐀⁡(x,t)​𝑑x\bar{\mathbf{A}}_{U}(t)=\fint_{U}{\mathbf{A}(x,t)\,dx}.

Definition 1.4.

For δ,R>0\delta,R>0, we say that Ω\Omega is (δ,R)(\delta,R)-Lipschitz if for every x0∈∂Ωx_{0}\in\partial\Omega there exists a Lipschitz continuous function γ:ℝn−1→ℝ\gamma:{\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}\to{\mathbb{R}} such that - upon relabeling and reorienting the coordinate axes - we have

Ω∩BR​(x0)={(x′,xn)∈BR​(x0):xn>γ⁡(x′)}\Omega\cap B_{R}(x_{0})=\big\{(x^{\prime},x_{n})\in B_{R}(x_{0}):\,x_{n}>\gamma(x^{\prime})\big\}

and

Lip(γ)=⁣=defsup{|γ⁡(x′)−γ⁡(y′)||x′−y′|:(x′,γ(x′)),(y′,γ(y′))∈BR(x0),x′≠y′}≤δ.\text{Lip}(\gamma)\mathbin{\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathbin{=\kern-2.0pt=}}\limits^{\rm def}}}\sup\Big\{\frac{|\gamma(x^{\prime})-\gamma(y^{\prime})|}{|x^{\prime}-y^{\prime}|}:(x^{\prime},\gamma(x^{\prime})),\,(y^{\prime},\gamma(y^{\prime}))\in B_{R}(x_{0}),x^{\prime}\neq y^{\prime}\Big\}\leq\delta.

Our main result on the regularity of solutions to (1.4) is the following theorem:

Theorem 1.5.

Let n≥2n\geq 2, T>0T>0, α≥0,λ>0\alpha\geq 0,\lambda>0, 0<θ≤10<\theta\leq 1, and 𝐀\mathbf{A} satisfy (1.5). Assume that cc is a non-negative function in Lp​(ΩT)L^{p}(\Omega_{T}) for some p>2p>2. There exists a number δ=δ⁡(p,R,Λ,α,n)>0\delta=\delta(p,R,\Lambda,\alpha,n)>0 such that if Ω\Omega is (δ,R)(\delta,R)-Lipschitz and [𝐀]B​M​O​(R,ΩT)≤δ[\mathbf{A}]_{BMO(R,\Omega_{T})}\leq\delta, then any weak solution uu of the problem (1.4) with 0≤u≤λ−10\leq u\leq\lambda^{-1} in ΩT\Omega_{T} satisfies

(1.6) ∫Ω×[t¯,T]|∇u|p​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡{(θλ∨‖u‖L2​(ΩT))p+∫ΩT|c|p​𝑑x​𝑑t}\int_{\Omega\times[\bar{t},T]}|\nabla u|^{p}\,dxdt\leq C\left\{\Big(\frac{\theta}{\lambda}\vee\|u\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}\Big)^{p}+\int_{\Omega_{T}}|c|^{p}\,dxdt\right\}

for every t¯∈(0,T)\bar{t}\in(0,T). Here C>0C>0 is a constant depending only on Ω\Omega, t¯\bar{t}, pp, RR, Λ\Lambda, nn and α\alpha, but independent of θ,λ\theta,\lambda.

We remark that the condition 0≤u≤λ−10\leq u\leq\lambda^{-1} is natural to ensure that the equation is uniformly parabolic, and is not restrictive for applications (see Lemma 3.2). It is also worth mentioning that W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates for linear parabolic equations are obtained in [4, 5, 6].

The proof of Theorem 1.5 is given in Section 2. We employ the perturbation technique introduced by Caffarelli-Peral [9] for equations in divergent form. Similar approach is also used in [4, 5, 6, 26]. This technique is a variation of the method developed by Caffarelli [7] for fully nonlinear uniformly elliptic equations (see also [8]). We note that the second equation in (1.3) is not invariant with respect to the scalings u⁡(x,t)→s−1​u​(s​x,s2​t)u(x,t)\rightarrow s^{-1}u(sx,s^{2}t) and u⁡(x,t)→r−1​u​(x,t)u(x,t)\rightarrow r^{-1}u(x,t) for s,r>0s,r>0. It is also not invariant with respect to the transformation that flattens the boundary of Ω\Omega. This presents a serious problem in establishing global W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates without assuming any smallness condition on the relevant functions. We handle this by introducing the pair of constants λ,θ\lambda,\theta and the coefficient matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} into (1.4) to ensure that this class of equations is invariant under the mentioned scalings and transformation. The parameters λ\lambda and θ\theta play a key role in our approach. On the other hand, this creates technical difficulties in obtaining approximation estimates that are uniformly in both λ\lambda and θ\theta (Lemmas 2.11 and 2.21). We overcome this by delicate analysis combining compactness argument with energy estimates.

Next, we outline our strategy for proving Theorem 1.2. First note that the equation of vv in (1.3) can be written in the form (1.4). Therefore, if u∈Lp​(ΩT)u\in L^{p}(\Omega_{T}), for some p>2p>2, we can apply Theorem 1.5 to derive the LpL^{p}-estimates for ∇v\nabla v. Using this new information in the equation of uu, we establish the LqL^{q}-estimates for uu with some q>pq>p depending on pp. We then repeat the process using the improved estimate u∈Lqu\in L^{q} and applying Theorem 1.5 to the equation of vv to gain ∇v∈Lq\nabla v\in L^{q}, and so on. With such iteration, we are able to obtain ∇v,u∈Lq\nabla v,u\in L^{q} for sufficiently large q∈(2,∞)q\in(2,\infty). Combining this with the classical regularity and the known results in [17, 33, 34], we derive a contradiction to (1.2). The full proof of Theorem 1.2 will be given in Section 3.

We close the introduction by noting that the partial differential equations in (1.3) can be rewritten in the following divergence form:

(1.7) u→t=∇⋅[J(x,t,u→)∇u→]+f(x,t,u→),\vec{u}_{t}=\nabla\cdot[J(x,t,\vec{u})\,\nabla\vec{u}]+f(x,t,\vec{u}),

where

u→=[uv]andJ⁡(x,t,u→)=[d1+2​a11​u+a12​va12​v0d2+2​a22​v].\vec{u}=\begin{bmatrix}u\\ v\end{bmatrix}\quad\text{and}\quad J(x,t,\vec{u})=\begin{bmatrix}d_{1}+2a_{11}u+a_{12}v&a_{12}v\\ 0&d_{2}+2a_{22}v\end{bmatrix}.

Equations of the general form (1.7) appear frequently in many areas of physical and biological applications with different types of nonlinearities for JJ and ff (see, for examples, [16, 24, 25, 35, 37]). In the simple case when JJ is independent of u→\vec{u}, they become the standard reaction-diffusion equations and have been studied extensively in the theory of parabolic equations (see [16, 23]). In our case, the dependence of JJ on u→\vec{u} creates mathematical and physical interesting phenomena and great technical complications. Although we focus only on the explicit system (1.3), the method in this paper might be extended to study general systems of form (1.7) with some structural conditions on JJ and ff.

2. Regularity of Solutions to Self-Diffusion Equations

2.1. Existence and uniqueness of weak solutions

This subsection proves the existence and uniqueness of solution of (1.4). We first introduce some notation. Let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be an open bounded Lipschitz domain, T>0T>0 and ΩT=Ω×(0,T]\Omega_{T}=\Omega\times(0,T]. Let Γ\Gamma be a relatively open connected subset of ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Denote

∂DΩT=Γ×(0,T)∪Ω×{0},∂NΩT=(∂Ω∖Γ)×(0,T),∂pΩT=∂Ω×(0,T)∪Ω×{0}.\partial_{D}\Omega_{T}=\Gamma\times(0,T)\cup\Omega\times\{0\},\quad\partial_{N}\Omega_{T}=(\partial\Omega\setminus\Gamma)\times(0,T),\quad\partial_{p}\Omega_{T}=\partial\Omega\times(0,T)\cup\Omega\times\{0\}.

We also denote the following spaces

H^01(Ω)={u∈H1(Ω):u=0onΓ},\hat{H}_{0}^{1}(\Omega)=\{u\in H^{1}(\Omega):u=0\quad\text{on}\quad\Gamma\},
𝒲⁡(ΩT)={u∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω)):ut∈L2​(0,T,H−1​(Ω))},\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T})=\big\{u\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)):u_{t}\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{-1}(\Omega))\big\},
(2.1) 𝒲^​(ΩT)={u∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω)):ut∈L2​(0,T,H^−1​(Ω))},\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})=\big\{u\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)):u_{t}\in L^{2}(0,T;\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega))\big\},

where H−1=(H01)∗H^{-1}=(H^{1}_{0})^{*} and H^−1=(H^01)∗\hat{H}^{-1}=(\hat{H}_{0}^{1})^{*}. Moreover, the spaces 𝒲⁡(ΩT)\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T}) and 𝒲^​(ΩT)\mathcal{\hat{W}}(\Omega_{T}) are endowed with the following norms:

‖u‖𝒲⁡(ΩT)=‖u‖L2​(ΩT)+‖∇u‖L2​(ΩT)+‖ut‖L2​(0,T,H−1​(Ω)),\left\|u\right\|_{\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T})}=\left\|u\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}+\left\|\nabla u\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}+\left\|u_{t}\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;H^{-1}(\Omega))},
‖u‖W^​(ΩT)=‖u‖L2​(ΩT)+‖∇u‖L2​(ΩT)+‖ut‖L2​(0,T,H^−1​(Ω)).\left\|u\right\|_{\hat{W}(\Omega_{T})}=\left\|u\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}+\left\|\nabla u\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}+\left\|u_{t}\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega))}.

Note that 𝒲^​(ΩT)⊂𝒲⁡(ΩT)\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})\subset\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T}), and 𝒲^​(ΩT)=𝒲⁡(ΩT)\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})=\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T}) when Γ=∂Ω\Gamma=\partial\Omega. It is well-known that the embedding

𝒲⁡(ΩT)↪C⁡([0,T],L2​(Ω))​ is continuous,{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})\hookrightarrow C([0,T];L^{2}(\Omega))\text{ is continuous},

and the embedding

(2.2) 𝒲⁡(ΩT)↪L2​(ΩT)​ is compact.{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\Omega_{T})\text{ is compact}.

Therefore, if u∈𝒲⁡(ΩT)u\in\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T}) then u⁡(⋅,t)u(\cdot,t) is well-defined and in L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) for each t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. Since 𝒲^​(ΩT)⊂𝒲⁡(ΩT)\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})\subset\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T}), these statements also hold true for 𝒲^​(ΩT)\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) in place of 𝒲⁡(ΩT)\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T}). Finally, for the spaces of test functions, we define

ℰ0(ΩT)={φ∈L2(0,T;H1(Ω)):φ=0on ∂pΩT},{\mathcal{E}}_{0}(\Omega_{T})=\{\varphi\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)):\varphi=0\quad\text{on }\partial_{p}\Omega_{T}\},
ℰ^0(ΩT)={φ∈L2(0,T;H1(Ω)):φ=0on ∂DΩT}.\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{0}(\Omega_{T})=\{\varphi\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)):\varphi=0\quad\text{on }\partial_{D}\Omega_{T}\}.
Definition 2.1.

Let g∈𝒲⁡(ΩT)g\in\mathcal{W}(\Omega_{T}), f∈L2​(0,T,H^−1​(Ω))f\in L^{2}(0,T;\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega)) and 𝐀\mathbf{A} satisfy (1.5). Let α≥θ≥0\alpha\geq\theta\geq 0 and let cc be a measurable function on ΩT\Omega_{T}.

    (2.3) ∫0T⟨ut,φ⟩H−1,H01dt+∫ΩT{(1+αu)⟨𝐀∇u,∇φ⟩−[θu(1−u)−cu]φ}dxdt−∫0T⟨f,φ⟩H^−1,H^01dt=0,\int_{0}^{T}\langle u_{t},\varphi\rangle_{H^{-1},H_{0}^{1}}dt+\int_{\Omega_{T}}\Big\{(1+\alpha u)\langle\mathbf{A}\nabla u,\nabla\varphi\rangle-[\theta u(1-u)-cu]\varphi\Big\}dxdt-\int_{0}^{T}\langle f,\varphi\rangle_{\hat{H}^{-1},\hat{H}_{0}^{1}}dt=0,

In fact, (2.3) is equivalent to the following variational formulation: for any v∈H01​(Ω)v\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega) and almost every t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T) one has

⟨ut,v⟩H−1,H01+((1+αu)𝐀∇u,∇v)L2​(Ω)=(θu(1−u)−cu,v)L2​(Ω)+⟨f,v⟩H^−1,H^01.\langle u_{t},v\rangle_{H^{-1},H_{0}^{1}}+((1+\alpha u)\mathbf{A}\nabla u,\nabla v)_{L^{2}(\Omega)}=(\theta u(1-u)-cu,v)_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\langle f,v\rangle_{\hat{H}^{-1},\hat{H}_{0}^{1}}.

From now on, if there is no confusion, we drop the subscripts H−1,H01H^{-1},H_{0}^{1} and H^−1,H^01\hat{H}^{-1},\hat{H}_{0}^{1} for the product notation ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle. In the statements above and calculations below, ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is also used to denote the scalar product in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, but its meaning is clear in the context.

We now can state the main theorem of this subsection.

Theorem 2.2.

Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} satisfy (1.5). Suppose the numbers α,θ\alpha,\theta are non-negative, c∈L2​(ΩT)c\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}) is non-negative, and g∈𝒲^​(ΩT)g\in\hat{{\mathcal{W}}}(\Omega_{T}) satisfies 0≤g≤10\leq g\leq 1. Then there exists a unique weak solution u∈𝒲^​(ΩT)u\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}), 0≤u≤10\leq u\leq 1 of the equation

(2.6) {ut=∇⋅[(1+αu)𝐀∇u]+θu(1−u)−cuinΩT,u=gon∂DΩT,∂u∂ν→=0,on∂NΩT.\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot[(1+\alpha u)\mathbf{A}\nabla u]+\theta u(1-u)-cu&\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega_{T},\\ u&=g&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{D}\Omega_{T},\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\vec{\nu}}&=0,&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{N}\Omega_{T}.\end{array}\right.

Moreover, there is a constant C=C⁡(T,Λ,α,θ)C=C(T,\Lambda,\alpha,\theta) such that

(2.7) sup0≤t≤T∫Ωu2​(x,t)​𝑑x+∫ΩT|∇u|2​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡[|Ω|+‖c‖L2​(ΩT)2+‖g‖𝒲^​(ΩT)2].\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\int_{\Omega}u^{2}(x,t)dx+\int_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla u|^{2}dxdt\leq C\Big[|\Omega|+\left\|c\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+\left\|g\right\|_{\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}\Big].

We prove the uniqueness first. This plays a key role in the existence of solutions to (2.6) and in our paper.

Lemma 2.3.

Let 𝐀,α,θ,c,g\mathbf{A},\alpha,\theta,c,g be as in Theorem 2.2. Then (2.6) has at most one weak solution u∈𝒲^​(ΩT)u\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) with 0≤u≤10\leq u\leq 1.

Suppose u1,u2∈𝒲^​(ΩT)u_{1},u_{2}\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) are two weak solutions of (2.6) satisfying 0≤u1,u2≤10\leq u_{1},u_{2}\leq 1. Let

Hence by using sgnk+​(w)\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w) as a test function in equation (2.6) for u1,u2u_{1},\,u_{2} and using integration by parts, one gets

∫Ω(u1−u2)tsgn+k(w)dx=−∫Ω⟨𝐀(x,t)[(1+αu1)∇u1−(1+αu2)∇u2],∇[sgn+k(w)]⟩dx+θ∫Ω(u1−u2)(1−u1−u2)sgn+k(w)dx−∫Ωc(u1−u2)sgn+k(w)dx=−∫Ω⟨𝐀(x,t)∇w,∇w⟩(sgn+k)′(w)dx+θ∫Ω(u1−u2)(1−u1−u2)sgn+k(w)dx−∫Ωc(u1−u2)sgn+k(w)dx.\begin{split}&\int_{\Omega}(u_{1}-u_{2})_{t}\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx=-\int_{\Omega}\langle\mathbf{A}(x,t)\big[(1+\alpha u_{1})\nabla u_{1}-(1+\alpha u_{2})\nabla u_{2}\big],\nabla[\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)]\rangle dx\\ &\quad\quad+\theta\int_{\Omega}(u_{1}-u_{2})(1-u_{1}-u_{2})\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx-\int_{\Omega}c(u_{1}-u_{2})\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx\\ &=-\int_{\Omega}\langle\mathbf{A}(x,t)\nabla w,\nabla w\rangle(\text{sgn}^{+}_{k})^{\prime}(w)dx+\theta\int_{\Omega}(u_{1}-u_{2})(1-u_{1}-u_{2})\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx\\ &\quad\quad\quad-\int_{\Omega}c(u_{1}-u_{2})\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx.\end{split}

As 𝐀⁡(x,t)\mathbf{A}(x,t) is non-negative definite and (sgnk+)′≥0(\text{sgn}^{+}_{k})^{\prime}\geq 0, we deduce that

∫Ω(u1−u2)t​sgnk+​(w)​𝑑x≤θ​∫Ω(u1−u2)​(1−u1−u2)​sgnk+​(w)​𝑑x−∫Ωc⁡(u1−u2)​sgnk+​(w)​𝑑x.\int_{\Omega}(u_{1}-u_{2})_{t}\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx\leq\theta\int_{\Omega}(u_{1}-u_{2})(1-u_{1}-u_{2})\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx-\int_{\Omega}c(u_{1}-u_{2})\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)dx.

Letting k→∞k\rightarrow\infty and observing that sgn+​(w)=sgn+​(u1−u2)\text{sgn}^{+}(w)=\text{sgn}^{+}(u_{1}-u_{2}), we obtain

yielding

A modification of the proof of Lemma 2.3 gives the following comparison principle:

Lemma 2.4.

Assume that 𝐀\mathbf{A} satisfies (1.5). Suppose that c∈L2​(ΩT)c\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}) is non-negative, g∈𝒲⁡(ΩT)g\in{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) and f∈L2​(0,T,H^−1​(Ω))f\in L^{2}(0,T;\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega)). Let u1,u2∈𝒲^​(ΩT)u_{1},u_{2}\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) be respectively weak sub-solution and weak super-solution to the problem

{ut=∇⋅[𝐀∇u]−cu+finΩT,u=gon∂DΩT,∂u∂ν→=0,on∂NΩT.\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot[\mathbf{A}\nabla u]-cu+f&\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega_{T},\\ u&=g&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{D}\Omega_{T},\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial\vec{\nu}}&=0,&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{N}\Omega_{T}.\\ \end{array}\right.

That is, (u1−g)+∈ℰ^0​(ΩT)(u_{1}-g)^{+}\in\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{0}(\Omega_{T}), (g−u2)+∈ℰ^0​(ΩT)(g-u_{2})^{+}\in\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{0}(\Omega_{T}) and for every function φ∈ℰ^0​(ΩT)\varphi\in\hat{\mathcal{E}}_{0}(\Omega_{T}) with φ≥0\varphi\geq 0, we have

∫0T⟨(u1)t,φ⟩dt≤∫ΩT{−⟨𝐀∇u1,∇φ⟩+[θu1(1−u1)−cu1]φ}dxdt+∫0T⟨f,φ⟩dt\int_{0}^{T}\langle(u_{1})_{t},\varphi\rangle dt\leq\int_{\Omega_{T}}\Big\{-\langle\mathbf{A}\nabla u_{1},\nabla\varphi\rangle+[\theta u_{1}(1-u_{1})-cu_{1}]\varphi\Big\}dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\langle f,\varphi\rangle dt

and

∫0T⟨(u2)t,φ⟩dt≥∫ΩT{−⟨𝐀∇u2,∇φ⟩+[θu2(1−u2)−cu2]φ}dxdt+∫0T⟨f,φ⟩dt.\int_{0}^{T}\langle(u_{2})_{t},\varphi\rangle dt\geq\int_{\Omega_{T}}\Big\{-\langle\mathbf{A}\nabla u_{2},\nabla\varphi\rangle+[\theta u_{2}(1-u_{2})-cu_{2}]\varphi\Big\}dxdt+\int_{0}^{T}\langle f,\varphi\rangle dt.

Then u1≤u2u_{1}\leq u_{2} almost everywhere on ΩT\Omega_{T}.

Let w=u1−u2w=u_{1}-u_{2}. Then w≤0w\leq 0 on ∂DΩT\partial_{D}\Omega_{T} since u1≤g≤u2u_{1}\leq g\leq u_{2} on ∂DΩT\partial_{D}\Omega_{T}. Hence sgnk+​(w)∈L2​(0,T,H1​(Ω))\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)\in L^{2}(0,T;H^{1}(\Omega)) with sgnk+​(w)=0\text{sgn}^{+}_{k}(w)=0 on ∂DΩT\partial_{D}\Omega_{T}, where sgnk+\text{sgn}^{+}_{k} is the function given by (2.8). Therefore, by arguing as in the proof of Lemma 2.3 we obtain

∫Ω(u1​(x,t)−u2​(x,t))+​𝑑x≤∫Ω(u1​(x,0)−u2​(x,0))+​𝑑xfor every ​t>0.\int_{\Omega}\Big(u_{1}(x,t)-u_{2}(x,t)\Big)^{+}dx\leq\int_{\Omega}\Big(u_{1}(x,0)-u_{2}(x,0)\Big)^{+}dx\quad\mbox{for every }t>0.

Next, we prove the energy estimate (2.7).

Lemma 2.5.

Let 𝐀,α,θ,g,c\mathbf{A},\alpha,\theta,g,c be as in Theorem 2.2, and f∈L2​(0,T,H^−1​(Ω))f\in L^{2}(0,T;\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega)). Suppose u∈𝒲^​(ΩT)u\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) is a weak solution of (2.4) with 0≤u≤10\leq u\leq 1. Then there exists C>0C>0 depending only on TT, Λ\Lambda, α\alpha and θ\theta such that

(2.9) sup0≤t≤T∫Ωu2​𝑑x+∫ΩT|∇u|2​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡[|Ω|+‖c‖L2​(ΩT)2+‖f‖L2​(0,T,H^−1​(Ω))2+‖g‖𝒲^​(ΩT)2].\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\int_{\Omega}u^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla u|^{2}dxdt\leq C\Big[|\Omega|+\left\|c\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+\left\|f\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T;\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega))}^{2}+\left\|g\right\|_{\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}\Big].

This can be rewritten as

+∫Ωθ(1−u)w2dx+∫Ωθ(1−u)gwdx−∫Ωcuwdx+⟨f,w⟩.\displaystyle\quad+\int_{\Omega}\theta(1-u)w^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}\theta(1-u)gwdx-\int_{\Omega}cuwdx+\langle f,w\rangle.

Using this together with (1.5), Cauchy-Schwartz inequality and the assumption 0≤u≤10\leq u\leq 1, we get

dd​t​∫Ωw2​𝑑x+Λ−1​∫Ω|∇w|2​𝑑x≤C[∫Ωg2dx+∫Ω|∇g|2dx+∫Ωc2(x,t)dx+(‖f(⋅,t)‖H^−1​(Ω)+‖gt(⋅,t)‖H^−1​(Ω))(‖w‖L2+‖∇w‖L2)+∫Ωw2dx],\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}w^{2}dx+\Lambda^{-1}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w|^{2}dx&\leq C\Big[\int_{\Omega}g^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla g|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}c^{2}(x,t)dx\\ &\quad+\big(\left\|f(\cdot,t)\right\|_{\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega)}+\left\|g_{t}(\cdot,t)\right\|_{\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega)}\big)\big(\left\|w\right\|_{L^{2}}+\left\|\nabla w\right\|_{L^{2}}\big)+\int_{\Omega}w^{2}dx\Big],\end{split}

where C>0C>0 depends only on Λ\Lambda, α\alpha and θ\theta. Hence

dd​t​∫Ωw2​𝑑x+(2​Λ)−1​∫Ω|∇w|2​𝑑x\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}w^{2}dx+(2\Lambda)^{-1}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w|^{2}dx
≤C⁡[‖c⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​(Ω)2+‖f⁡(⋅,t)‖H^−1​(Ω)2+(‖g⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​(Ω)2+‖∇g​(⋅,t)‖L2​(Ω)2+‖gt​(⋅,t)‖H^−1​(Ω)2)+∫Ωw2​𝑑x].\displaystyle\leq C\Big[\|c(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\left\|f(\cdot,t)\right\|_{\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega)}^{2}+\Big(\|g(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\|\nabla g(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{2}+\left\|g_{t}(\cdot,t)\right\|_{\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega)}^{2}\Big)+\int_{\Omega}w^{2}dx\Big].

for some constant C=C⁡(T,Λ,α,θ)C=C(T,\Lambda,\alpha,\theta). Since 0≤g≤10\leq g\leq 1, we therefore obtain the estimate (2.9). ∎

We also need the following result for linear parabolic equations with mixed boundary conditions.

Lemma 2.6.

Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} satisfy (1.5) and c,f∈L2​(ΩT)c,f\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}) with 0≤f≤c0\leq f\leq c. Suppose g∈𝒲^​(ΩT)g\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) with 0≤g≤10\leq g\leq 1. Then there exists a unique weak solution w∈𝒲^​(ΩT)w\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) of the problem

(2.10) {wt=∇⋅[𝐀∇w]−cw+finΩT,w=gon∂DΩT,∂w∂ν→=0on∂NΩT.\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcll}w_{t}&=&\nabla\cdot[\mathbf{A}\nabla w]-cw+f&\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega_{T},\\ w&=&g&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{D}\Omega_{T},\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial w}{\partial\vec{\nu}}&=&0&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{N}\Omega_{T}.\end{array}\right.

Moreover, 0≤w≤10\leq w\leq 1.

Proof.

For each k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, let ck=min⁡{c,k}c_{k}=\min\{c,k\} and fk=min⁡{f,k}f_{k}=\min\{f,k\}. From the standard theory of linear parabolic equations in divergence forms with bounded coefficients (see, for example, [28, Theorem 9.9]), there exists a unique weak solution wk∈𝒲^​(ΩT)w_{k}\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) of the approximation problem

(2.11) {∂twk=∇⋅[𝐀∇wk]−ckwk+fkinΩT,wk=gon∂DΩT,∂wk∂ν→=0on∂NΩT.\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcll}\partial_{t}w_{k}&=&\nabla\cdot[\mathbf{A}\nabla w_{k}]-c_{k}w_{k}+f_{k}&\quad\text{in}\quad\Omega_{T},\\ w_{k}&=&g&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{D}\Omega_{T},\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial w_{k}}{\partial\vec{\nu}}&=&0&\quad\text{on}\quad\partial_{N}\Omega_{T}.\end{array}\right.

Since 0≤fk≤ck0\leq f_{k}\leq c_{k} and 0≤g≤10\leq g\leq 1, we see that u1=0u_{1}=0 is a weak sub-solution and u2=1u_{2}=1 is a weak super-solution to the problem (2.11). Therefore, it follows from Lemma 2.4 that

0≤wk≤1inΩT,∀k∈ℕ.0\leq w_{k}\leq 1\quad\mbox{in}\quad\Omega_{T},\quad\forall k\in\mathbb{N}.

Also by Lemma 2.5, we obtain

sup0≤t≤T∫Ω|wk|2​𝑑x+∫ΩT|∇wk|2​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡[|Ω|+‖ck‖L2​(ΩT)2+‖fk‖L2​(ΩT)2+‖g‖𝒲^​(ΩT)2]≤C⁡[|Ω|+‖c‖L2​(ΩT)2+‖f‖L2​(ΩT)2+‖g‖𝒲^​(ΩT)2].\begin{split}\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\int_{\Omega}|w_{k}|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla w_{k}|^{2}dxdt&\leq C\Big[|\Omega|+\left\|c_{k}\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+\left\|f_{k}\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+\left\|g\right\|_{\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}\Big]\\ &\leq C\Big[|\Omega|+\left\|c\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+\left\|f\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}+\left\|g\right\|_{\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})}^{2}\Big].\end{split}

This together with (2.11) and the boundedness of wkw_{k} yield

‖wk‖𝒲^​(ΩT)≤C,∀k∈ℕ.\left\|w_{k}\right\|_{\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C,\quad\forall\ k\in\mathbb{N}.

By the compact embedding (2.2) and the fact that {ck​wk}\{c_{k}w_{k}\} is bounded in L2​(0,T,ΩT)L^{2}(0,T;\Omega_{T}), there is a subsequence, still denoted by {wk}\{w_{k}\}, and a function w∈𝒲^​(ΩT)w\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) such that

{wk→w​ strongly in ​L2​(ΩT),ckwk⇀cwand∇wk⇀∇w weakly in L2(ΩT),∂twk⇀∂tw​ weakly-* in ​L2​(0,T,H^−1​(ΩT)).\left\{\ \begin{array}[]{lll}&w_{k}\to w\mbox{ strongly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T}),\\ &c_{k}w_{k}\rightharpoonup cw\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla w_{k}\rightharpoonup\nabla w\text{ weakly in }L^{2}(\Omega_{T}),\\ &\partial_{t}w_{k}\rightharpoonup\partial_{t}w\text{ weakly-* in }L^{2}(0,T;\hat{H}^{-1}(\Omega_{T})).\end{array}\right.

Clearly, 0≤w≤10\leq w\leq 1. Now, by taking k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, it follows from (2.11) that ww is a weak solution of (2.10). The uniqueness of the solution ww is guaranteed by Lemma 2.4. ∎

Now, we are ready to prove Theorem 2.2.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.

Thanks to Lemma 2.3 and Lemma 2.5, it remains to prove the existence of a weak solution u∈𝒲^​(ΩT)u\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) to (2.6) satisfying 0≤u≤10\leq u\leq 1. We give the proof for the case θ>0\theta>0. The case θ=0\theta=0 is similar and, in fact, simpler. Without loss of generality, let us assume θ=1\theta=1. The proof is based on the Schauder fixed point theorem. Alternatively, one can also use the iterative monotone method based on lower and upper solutions (see [29]). Define

E={v∈L2​(ΩT):0≤v≤1},f⁡(s)=2​s−s2,E=\{v\in L^{2}(\Omega_{T}):0\leq v\leq 1\},\quad f(s)=2s-s^{2},

and let

𝕃v[w]=∇⋅[(1+αv)𝐀∇w]−(c+1)w.\mathbb{L}_{v}[w]=\nabla\cdot[(1+\alpha v)\mathbf{A}\nabla w]-(c+1)w.

Note that the function f⁡(s)f(s) is increasing on [0,1][0,1]. Hence

0≤f⁡(v)≤f⁡(1)=1≤c+1,∀v∈E.0\leq f(v)\leq f(1)=1\leq c+1,\quad\forall\ v\in E.

Therefore, it follows from Lemma 2.6 that for each v∈Ev\in E, there exists a unique weak solution w∈𝒲^​(ΩT)w\in\hat{\mathcal{W}}(\Omega_{T}) with 0≤w≤10\leq w\leq 1 of the problem

Thus, we can define the map ℒ:E→E⊂L2​(ΩT)\mathcal{L}:E\rightarrow E\subset L^{2}(\Omega_{T}) by ℒ⁡(v)=w\mathcal{L}(v)=w, for each v∈Ev\in E, where ww is the solution of (2.12). It is clear that EE is a closed, convex set in L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T}). We now seek for u∈Eu\in E such that u=ℒ⁡(u)u=\mathcal{L}(u). By [14, Corollary 11.2], it suffices to show that ℒ\mathcal{L} is completely continuous. Note that from Lemma 2.5, there is C=C⁡(T,Λ)C=C(T,\Lambda) such that

From this and the compact imbedding (2.2), we conclude that ℒ⁡(E)\mathcal{L}(E) is pre-compact in L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T}). Therefore, it remains to show that ℒ\mathcal{L} is continuous in L2​(ΩT)L^{2}(\Omega_{T})-topology. From (2.14), we have

2.4. Global W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates on Lipschitz domains

In this subsection we consider the Neumann problem (1.4) and derive global W1,pW^{1,p}-estimates for the solution uu. To this end, we will flatten the boundary of the domain Ω\Omega and then employ Theorem 2.26.

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

0≤v⁡(x,t)≤M0:=max⁡{a2c2,maxΩ¯⁡v0},∀(x,t)∈Ω×[0,T).0\leq v(x,t)\leq M_{0}:=\max\Big\{\frac{a_{2}}{c_{2}},\max_{\overline{\Omega}}v_{0}\Big\},\quad\forall\ (x,t)\in\Omega\times[0,T).

sup0≤t≤T∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x≤C⁡(T).\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx\leq C(T).

Then the interpolation inequality yields

∫Ωw⁡(x,t)​𝑑x≤‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L1​(Ω)λ⁡(q+1)2​‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖Lq¯​(Ω)1−λ≤C⁡(T)​‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖Lq¯​(Ω)1−λwith1−λq¯+λ2q+1=1.\int_{\Omega}w(x,t)dx\leq\left\|u(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}^{\frac{\lambda(q+1)}{2}}\left\|w(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\bar{q}}(\Omega)}^{1-\lambda}\leq C(T)\left\|w(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\bar{q}}(\Omega)}^{1-\lambda}\quad\text{with}\quad\frac{1-\lambda}{\bar{q}}+\frac{\lambda}{\frac{2}{q+1}}=1.

This, together with (3.7) and Young’s inequality imply that

‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖Lq¯​(Ω)≤C⁡{‖∇w​(⋅,t)‖L2​(Ω)2q¯​‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​qq+1​(Ω)4​qn⁡(q+1)​q¯+1}.\left\|w(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\bar{q}}(\Omega)}\leq C\left\{\left\|\nabla w(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}^{\frac{2}{\bar{q}}}\left\|w(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\frac{2q}{q+1}}(\Omega)}^{\frac{4q}{n(q+1)\bar{q}}}+1\right\}.

Therefore,

(3.8) ‖w‖Lq¯​(ΩT1)≤C⁡[‖∇w‖L2​(ΩT1)2q¯​(sup0<t<T1‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​qq+1​(Ω))4​qn⁡(q+1)​q¯+1].\left\|w\right\|_{L^{\bar{q}}(\Omega_{T_{1}})}\leq C\left[\left\|\nabla w\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{T_{1}})}^{\frac{2}{\bar{q}}}\Big(\sup_{0<t<T_{1}}\left\|w(\cdot,t)\right\|_{L^{\frac{2q}{q+1}}(\Omega)}\Big)^{\frac{4q}{n(q+1)\bar{q}}}+1\right].

Also, since q∈(1,n⁡(p−1)(n+2−p)+]q\in\Big(1,\frac{n(p-1)}{(n+2-p)_{+}}\Big] and q≠∞q\not=\infty, we see that

(n​p¯−2​n−4)​q≤n⁡(p¯+2)andp¯​(q−1)q+1≤q¯.(n\bar{p}-2n-4)q\leq n(\bar{p}+2)\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\bar{p}(q-1)}{q+1}\leq\bar{q}.

From this and (3.8), we obtain

(3.9) ‖w‖L(q−1)​p¯q+1​(ΩT1)≤C​‖w‖Lq¯​(ΩT1)≤C⁡[1+E​(T1)2n​q¯+1q¯].\left\|w\right\|_{L^{\frac{(q-1)\bar{p}}{q+1}}(\Omega_{T_{1}})}\leq C\left\|w\right\|_{L^{\bar{q}}(\Omega_{T_{1}})}\leq C\Big[1+E(T_{1})^{\frac{2}{n\bar{q}}+\frac{1}{\bar{q}}}\Big].

Hence, it follows from this last inequality and (3.6) that

(3.10) E⁡(T1)≤C⁡[1+E​(T1)μ],withμ=2​(q−1)q¯​(q+1)​(2n+1)andC=C⁡(T).E(T_{1})\leq C[1+E(T_{1})^{\mu}],\quad\text{with}\quad\mu=\frac{2(q-1)}{\bar{q}(q+1)}\left(\frac{2}{n}+1\right)\quad\text{and}\quad C=C(T).

A simple calculation shows μ<1\mu<1. Because of this and the fact E⁡(T1)E(T_{1}) is finite, we infer from (3.10) that there exists a constant C⁡(T)C(T) such that

(3.11) E⁡(T1)≤C⁡(T),∀T1∈(0,T).E(T_{1})\leq C(T),\quad\forall\ T_{1}\in(0,T).

By passing T1→T−T_{1}\to T^{-}, we obtain the first inequality of (3.5). The second inequality of (3.5) follows directly from (3.9) and (3.11), and again, passing T1→T−T_{1}\to T^{-}. The proof is therefore complete. ∎

To initiate our iteration process, we start with the following L4L^{4}-estimate for ∇v\nabla v.

Lemma 3.5.

[34, Lemma 3.1] There exists a constant CC depending on TT, the coefficients in the system (1.3) and the initial data u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} such that

‖∇v‖L4​(ΩT)≤C.\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{L^{4}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C.

We now can combine the previous results to improve the regularity of uu and vv.

Lemma 3.6.

There exists a constant CC depending on TT such that

(3.12) sup0<t<T∫Ωu​(x,t)p0​𝑑x+∫ΩT|∇v​(x,t)|p0​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C.\sup_{0<t<T}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)^{p_{0}}dx+\int_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla v(x,t)|^{p_{0}}dxdt\leq C.

Moreover, for all finite p∈(2,p0​(n+1)(n+2−p0)+]p\in\Big(2,\frac{p_{0}(n+1)}{(n+2-p_{0})_{+}}\Big], there exists C=C⁡(p,T)C=C(p,T) such that

(3.13) ∫ΩTu​(x,t)p​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡(p,T).\int_{\Omega_{T}}u(x,t)^{p}dxdt\leq C(p,T).
Proof.

Since (3.13) follows (3.12) and the second inequality of (3.5) in Lemma 3.4, it suffices to prove (3.12) only. Let l1=4l_{1}=4.

Step 1. If l1≥min⁡{p0,n+2}l_{1}\geq\min\{p_{0},n+2\}, then (3.12) can be obtained directly from Lemmas 3.2 and 3.4. Now, we consider the case l1<min⁡{p0,n+2}l_{1}<\min\{p_{0},n+2\}. Note in this case that n>2n>2. We then infer from Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5 that

∫ΩT|u⁡(x,t)|l2​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡(T)withl2=l1​(n+1)(n+2−l1)+=l1​(n+1)n−2.\int_{\Omega_{T}}|u(x,t)|^{l_{2}}dxdt\leq C(T)\quad\text{with}\quad l_{2}=\frac{l_{1}(n+1)}{(n+2-l_{1})_{+}}=\frac{l_{1}(n+1)}{n-2}.

Step 2. If l2≥min⁡{p0,n+2}l_{2}\geq\min\{p_{0},n+2\}, we can use Lemmas 3.2 and 3.4 to obtain (3.12) and we then stop. We therefore only consider the case l2<min⁡{p0,n+2}l_{2}<\min\{p_{0},n+2\}. By Lemma 3.2, we see that

∫ΩT|∇v​(x,t)|l2​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡(T)<∞.\int_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla v(x,t)|^{l_{2}}dxdt\leq C(T)<\infty.

From this and Lemma 3.4, we have

∫ΩTul3​(x,t)​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C⁡(T)<∞withl3=l2​(n+1)n+2−l2.\int_{\Omega_{T}}u^{l_{3}}(x,t)dxdt\leq C(T)<\infty\quad\text{with}\quad l_{3}=\frac{l_{2}(n+1)}{n+2-l_{2}}.

Observe that

l3=l2​(n+1)n+2−l2>l2​(n+1)n−2=l1​(n+1n−2)2.l_{3}=\frac{l_{2}(n+1)}{n+2-l_{2}}>\frac{l_{2}(n+1)}{n-2}=l_{1}\Big(\frac{n+1}{n-2}\Big)^{2}.

We will repeat this procedure. For i≥3i\geq 3, define li+1=li​(n+1)n+2−li.\displaystyle l_{i+1}=\frac{l_{i}(n+1)}{n+2-l_{i}}. Then the sequence {li}i=1∞\{l_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty} is strictly increasing and

li+1≥l1​(n+1n−2)i∀i≥1.l_{i+1}\geq l_{1}\Big(\frac{n+1}{n-2}\Big)^{i}\quad\forall\ i\geq 1.

Hence limi→∞li=∞\lim_{i\to\infty}l_{i}=\infty. Let kk be the smallest integer in [2,∞)[2,\infty) such that lk≥min⁡{p0,n+2}l_{k}\geq\min\{p_{0},n+2\}.

We repeat Step 2 above with lil_{i}, for i=3,…,k−1i=3,\ldots,k-1, to arrive at Step (k−1)(k-1) and obtain

∫ΩT|∇v​(x,t)|li​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C∀i=1,⋯,k−1,and∫ΩT|u⁡(x,t)|lk​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C.\int_{\Omega_{T}}|\nabla v(x,t)|^{l_{i}}dxdt\leq C\quad\forall\ i=1,\cdots,k-1,\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\Omega_{T}}|u(x,t)|^{l_{k}}dxdt\leq C.

Since lk≥min⁡{p0,n+2}l_{k}\geq\min\{p_{0},n+2\}, we, again, obtain (3.12) from Lemmas 3.2 and 3.4. The proof is complete. ∎

The next estimate for ∇v\nabla v is crucial for obtaining the boundedness of uu.

Lemma 3.7.

There exists p1>n+2p_{1}>n+2 and a constant C⁡(T)>0C(T)>0 such that

(3.14) ‖∇v‖Lp1​(Ω×[t¯,T])≤C⁡(T).\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\Omega\times[\bar{t},T])}\leq C(T).

If n=2n=2, from Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5, we obtain

‖u‖Lp​(ΩT)≤C⁡(p,T),∀p∈(2,∞).\left\|u\right\|_{L^{p}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C(p,T),\quad\forall\ p\in(2,\infty).

This together with Theorem 1.5 imply that

‖∇v‖Lp​(Ω×[t¯,T])≤C⁡[1+‖u‖Lp​(ΩT)]≤C⁡(p,T),∀p∈[2,∞).\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{L^{p}(\Omega\times[\bar{t},T])}\leq C\Big[1+\left\|u\right\|_{L^{p}(\Omega_{T})}\Big]\leq C(p,T),\quad\forall\ p\in[2,\infty).

Hence we obtain (3.14) for n=2n=2. Now, consider n>2n>2. Since p0>np_{0}>n and n≥3n\geq 3, a simple calculation gives

p0​(n+1)(n+2−p0)+>n+2.\frac{p_{0}(n+1)}{(n+2-p_{0})_{+}}>n+2.

Therefore, it follows from Lemma 3.6 that there exists p1>n+2p_{1}>n+2 such that

‖u‖Lp1​(ΩT)≤C⁡(T).\left\|u\right\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C(T).

Then applying Theorem 1.5 again, we obtain

‖∇v‖Lp1​(Ω×[t¯,T]CLOSE≤C⁡[1+‖u‖Lp1​(ΩT)]≤C⁡(T),\left\|\nabla v\right\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\Omega\times[\bar{t},T]}\leq C\Big[1+\left\|u\right\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\Omega_{T})}\Big]\leq C(T),

which proves (3.14). ∎

We now show that uu is bounded:

Lemma 3.8.

There exists a constant C⁡(T)>0C(T)>0 such that

(3.15) ‖u‖L∞​(ΩT)≤C⁡(T).\left\|u\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C(T).

From Theorem 1.1, we have u∈C⁡([0,t¯],W1,p0​(Ω))u\in C([0,\bar{t}],W^{1,p_{0}}(\Omega)) with p0>np_{0}>n. By Morrey’s imbedding theorem, there exists C¯0=C¯0​(t¯)>0\bar{C}_{0}=\bar{C}_{0}(\bar{t})>0 such that

We thus only need to prove that uu is bounded in Ω×[t¯,T]\Omega\times[\bar{t},T]. For each t1∈(t¯,T]t_{1}\in(\bar{t},T], and each k>C¯0k>\bar{C}_{0}, denote Wk​(x,t)=max⁡{u⁡(x,t)−k,0}W_{k}(x,t)=\max\{u(x,t)-k,0\} and

Ωt1​(k)={(x,t)∈Ω×[t¯,t1]:u⁡(x,t)>k}.\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)=\{(x,t)\in\Omega\times[\bar{t},t_{1}]:u(x,t)>k\}.

We write the equation of uu as

(3.17) ut=∇⋅[A(x,t)∇u]+a12∇⋅[u∇v]+f(x,t)in ΩT,u_{t}=\nabla\cdot[A(x,t)\nabla u]+a_{12}\nabla\cdot[u\nabla v]+f(x,t)\quad\text{in }\Omega_{T},

with homogeneous Neumann boundary condition, where

(3.18) A⁡(x,t)=d1+2​a11​u​(x,t)+a1,2​v​(x,t),f⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x,t)​[a1−b1​u​(x,t)−c1​v​(x,t)].A(x,t)=d_{1}+2a_{11}u(x,t)+a_{1,2}v(x,t),\quad f(x,t)=u(x,t)[a_{1}-b_{1}u(x,t)-c_{1}v(x,t)].

We note that A⁡(x,t)A(x,t) is bounded below by d1>0d_{1}>0, and not known to be bounded above. However, we can follow the De Giorgi’s iteration technique [16, Theorem 7.1, p. 181] to prove (3.15). By multiplying the equation (3.17) with WkW_{k} and using the integration by parts, we obtain

12​∫ΩWk2​(x,t)​𝑑x+d1​∫Ωt1​(k)|∇Wk|2​𝑑x​𝑑t+a11​∫Ωt1​(k)|∇Wk|2​u​𝑑x​𝑑t≤2​a12​∫Ωt1​(k)|∇v||∇Wk|u​𝑑x​𝑑t+2​a1​∫Ωt1​(k)​(k)u​Wk​𝑑x​𝑑t≤d12∫Ωt1​(k)|∇Wk|2dxdt+C∫Ωt1​(k)[|∇v|2+1][Wk2+k2]dxdt,∀t∈[t¯,t1].\begin{split}&\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}W_{k}^{2}(x,t)dx+d_{1}\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)}|\nabla W_{k}|^{2}dxdt+a_{11}\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)}|\nabla W_{k}|^{2}udxdt\\ &\leq 2a_{12}\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)}|\nabla v||\nabla W_{k}|udxdt+2a_{1}\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)(k)}uW_{k}dxdt\\ &\leq\frac{d_{1}}{2}\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)}|\nabla W_{k}|^{2}dxdt+C\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)}\Big[|\nabla v|^{2}+1\Big]\Big[W_{k}^{2}+k^{2}\Big]dxdt,\quad\forall\ t\in[\bar{t},t_{1}].\end{split}

Therefore, there exists a constant C>0C>0 depending only on the coefficients d1d_{1} and a1,a11,a12a_{1},a_{11},a_{12} such that

(3.19) ‖Wk‖V22:=sup0<t<t1∫ΩWk2​(x,t)​𝑑x​𝑑t+∫Ω×(t¯,t1)|∇Wk​(x,t)|2​𝑑x​𝑑t≤C​∫Ωt1​(k)[|∇v​(x,t)|2+1]​[Wk2+k2]​dx​dt.\begin{split}\left\|W_{k}\right\|_{V_{2}}^{2}&:=\sup_{0<t<t_{1}}\int_{\Omega}W_{k}^{2}(x,t)dxdt+\int_{\Omega\times(\bar{t},t_{1})}|\nabla W_{k}(x,t)|^{2}dxdt\\ &\leq C\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)}\Big[|\nabla v(x,t)|^{2}+1\Big]\Big[W_{k}^{2}+k^{2}\Big]dxdt.\end{split}

We estimate the right hand side of (3.19). Let p1p_{1} be as in Lemma 3.7. Then by Hölder’s inequality and Lemma 3.7, we have

(3.20) ∫Ωt1​(k)[|∇v|2+1]​[Wk2+k2]​𝑑x​𝑑t≤‖|∇v|+1‖Lp1​(Ωt1​(k))2​‖Wk+k‖L2​p1p1−2​(Ωt1​(k))2≤C⁡(T)​[‖Wk‖L2​p1p1−2​(Ωt1​(k))2+k2​μ​(k)p1−2p1],\begin{split}\int_{\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)}[|\nabla v|^{2}+1][W_{k}^{2}+k^{2}]dxdt&\leq\left\|\,|\nabla v|+1\right\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\Omega_{t_{1}}(k))}^{2}\left\|W_{k}+k\right\|_{L^{\frac{2p_{1}}{p_{1}-2}}(\Omega_{t_{1}}(k))}^{2}\\ &\leq C(T)\left[\left\|W_{k}\right\|_{L^{\frac{2p_{1}}{p_{1}-2}}(\Omega_{t_{1}}(k))}^{2}+k^{2}\mu(k)^{\frac{p_{1}-2}{p_{1}}}\right],\end{split}

where μ⁡(k):=|Ωt1​(k)|\mu(k):=|\Omega_{t_{1}}(k)|. Observe that p1>n+2p_{1}>n+2 implies

p1p1−2<n+2n,henceδ:=p1−2p1−nn+2>0.\frac{p_{1}}{p_{1}-2}<\frac{n+2}{n},\quad\text{hence}\quad\delta:=\frac{p_{1}-2}{p_{1}}-\frac{n}{n+2}>0.

Therefore, we can apply Hölder’s inequality and then the parabolic imbedding theorem ([16, (3.4), p. 75] to infer that

(3.21) ‖Wk‖L2​p1p1−2​(Ωt1​(k))2≤‖Wk‖L2​(n+2)n​(Ωt1​(k))2​μ​(k)δ≤C⁡(T)​‖Wk‖V22​μ​(k)δ.\left\|W_{k}\right\|_{L^{\frac{2p_{1}}{p_{1}-2}}(\Omega_{t_{1}}(k))}^{2}\leq\left\|W_{k}\right\|_{L^{\frac{2(n+2)}{n}}(\Omega_{t_{1}}(k))}^{2}\mu(k)^{\delta}\leq C(T)\left\|W_{k}\right\|_{V_{2}}^{2}\mu(k)^{\delta}.

By (3.19), (3.20) and (3.21), there exists C1​(T)>0C_{1}(T)>0 such that

Let t1∈(t¯,T]t_{1}\in(\bar{t},T] satisfy C1​(T)​[|Ω|​(t1−t¯)]δ≤1/2C_{1}(T)\left[|\Omega|(t_{1}-\bar{t})\right]^{\delta}\leq 1/2. Then the inequality (3.22) yields

(3.23) ‖Wk‖V22≤2​C1​(T)​k2​μ​(k)p1−2p1.\begin{split}\left\|W_{k}\right\|_{V_{2}}^{2}\leq 2C_{1}(T)k^{2}\mu(k)^{\frac{p_{1}-2}{p_{1}}}.\end{split}

From this and the standard iteration technique ([16, Theorem 6.1, p. 102]), we deduce that

(3.24) supΩ×[t¯,t1]u⁡(x,t)≤C¯1.\sup_{\Omega\times[\bar{t},t_{1}]}u(x,t)\leq\bar{C}_{1}.

where C¯1=C¯1​(T)>0\bar{C}_{1}=\bar{C}_{1}(T)>0.

Now, partition the interval [t¯,T][\bar{t},T] evenly with

t¯=t0<t1<t2<⋯<tN+1=T,tj=t0+j​h,\bar{t}=t_{0}<t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots<t_{N+1}=T,\quad t_{j}=t_{0}+jh,

where the time step h>0h>0 is chosen to satisfy C1​(T)​[h​|Ω|]δ≤1/2C_{1}(T)[h\,|\Omega|]^{\delta}\leq 1/2. Repeating the proof of (3.24) on each time interval [tj,tj+1][t_{j},t_{j+1}] for j=1,2,⋯,Nj=1,2,\cdots,N, we obtain

(3.25) supΩ×[tj,tj+1]u⁡(x,t)≤C¯j+1,\sup_{\Omega\times[t_{j},t_{j+1}]}u(x,t)\leq\bar{C}_{j+1},

where C¯j+1=C¯j+1​(T)>0\bar{C}_{j+1}=\bar{C}_{j+1}(T)>0 also depends on the preceding bound C¯j\bar{C}_{j} on [tj−1,tj][t_{j-1},t_{j}]. (In the proof, we replace C¯0\bar{C}_{0} by C¯j\bar{C}_{j}.) Therefore, we obtain

(3.26) supΩ×[t¯,T]u≤C⁡(T).\sup_{\Omega\times[\bar{t},T]}u\leq C(T).

The estimate (3.15) then follows from (3.16) and (3.26). ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

For all (x,t)∈ΩT(x,t)\in\Omega_{T}, as in the proof of Lemma 3.8, let A⁡(x,t)A(x,t), f⁡(x,t)f(x,t) be defined by (3.18) and let

B⁡(x,t)=d2+2​a22​v​(x,t),g⁡(x,t)=v⁡(x,t)​[a2−b2​u​(x,t)−c2​v​(x,t)].B(x,t)=d_{2}+2a_{22}v(x,t),\quad g(x,t)=v(x,t)[a_{2}-b_{2}u(x,t)-c_{2}v(x,t)].

From Lemmas 3.1 and 3.8, there are constants Λ>0\Lambda>0 and C>0C>0 such that

(3.27) Λ−1≤A⁡(x,t)≤ΛandΛ−1≤B⁡(x,t)≤Λ∀(x,t)∈ΩT,\Lambda^{-1}\leq A(x,t)\leq\Lambda\quad\text{and}\quad\Lambda^{-1}\leq B(x,t)\leq\Lambda\quad\forall\ (x,t)\in\Omega_{T},
(3.28) ‖f‖L∞​(ΩT)+‖g‖L∞​(ΩT)≤C.\left\|f\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}+\left\|g\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C.

We rewrite the equation (3.1) as

vt=∇⋅[B(x,t)∇v]+g.v_{t}=\nabla\cdot[B(x,t)\nabla v]+g.

From (3.27), (3.28), and the classical Hölder regularity theory ([16, Theorem 10.1, p. 204], [12, Theorem 1.3, Remark 1.1, p. 43]), there exist α1∈(0,1)\alpha_{1}\in(0,1) and C⁡(T)>0C(T)>0 such that

(3.29) ‖v‖Cα1,α12​(Ω¯T)≤C⁡(T).\left\|v\right\|_{C^{\alpha_{1},\frac{\alpha_{1}}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}_{T})}\leq C(T).

Next, we rewrite the equation of uu as

(3.30) ut=∇⋅[A(x,t)∇u]+∇⋅F→1+∇⋅F→2+f,u_{t}=\nabla\cdot[A(x,t)\nabla u]+\nabla\cdot\vec{F}_{1}+\nabla\cdot\vec{F}_{2}+f,

where

F→1(x,t)=a12χ[0,t¯](t)u(x,t)∇v(x,t)andF→2(x,t)=a12χ[t¯,T](t)u(x,t)∇v(x,t).\vec{F}_{1}(x,t)=a_{12}\,\chi_{[0,\bar{t}]}(t)u(x,t)\nabla v(x,t)\quad\text{and}\quad\vec{F}_{2}(x,t)=a_{12}\,\chi_{[\bar{t},T]}(t)u(x,t)\nabla v(x,t).

Here, χI\chi_{I} denotes the characteristic function of the set I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R}. From Theorem 1.1, Lemmas 3.7 and 3.8, we see that

‖F→1‖L∞​([0,T],Lp0​(Ω))≤C⁡(t¯)and‖F→2‖Lp1​(ΩT)≤C⁡(T),\left\|\vec{F}_{1}\right\|_{L^{\infty}([0,T];L^{p_{0}}(\Omega))}\leq C(\bar{t})\quad\text{and}\quad\left\|\vec{F}_{2}\right\|_{L^{p_{1}}(\Omega_{T})}\leq C(T),

where p1>n+2p_{1}>n+2 is given by Lemma 3.7. Therefore, we can again apply the classical Hölder regularity theory ([16, Theorem 10.1, p. 204], [12, Theorem 1.3, Remark 1.1, p. 43]) to the equation (3.30) to infer that there are α2∈(0,1)\alpha_{2}\in(0,1) and C⁡(T)>0C(T)>0 such that

‖u‖Cα2,α22​(ΩT¯)≤C⁡(T).\left\|u\right\|_{C^{\alpha_{2},\frac{\alpha_{2}}{2}}(\overline{\Omega_{T}})}\leq C(T).

Let w=(d2+a22​v)​vw=(d_{2}+a_{22}v)v, then ww solves
